about: Learn's pages, release 1 (Oct 2026). Written fresh from the sources in sources.json; each fact lists the sources it comes from. Honesty labels: proven, tendency (strong tendency), trade (trade description), anecdotal, unproven.

entries.name: Caturra
entries.summary: A compact mutation of Bourbon found in Brazil.
entries.lede: A small, sturdy mutation of Bourbon found in Brazil about a century ago. It reached Central America in the 1940s and was once thought to make up nearly half of Colombia's coffee.

facts.label: found in Minas Gerais, Brazil
apart from Bourbon: a mutation that makes it a dwarf
does best high up; WCR rates its cup good
why Colombia replanted with resistant kinds

taste.text: That's how one participant in a Colombian trial described a good Caturra, next to Castillo's fruit, dark chocolate and roasted nut. Few sources say more, so treat it as a hint and trust what people here taste.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: In the few trials there are, where it's grown and how it's handled moved the cup as much as the variety did, or more.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: A dwarf Bourbon; a parent of Catuaí and the Catimors
body: Caturra is a natural mutation of Bourbon. A single gene makes the tree a dwarf; otherwise the two are so close genetically that they're told apart by how the plant grows.
It's a parent of Catuaí (Mundo Novo × Caturra, crossed in Brazil in 1949) and of the Catimors (Timor Hybrid × Caturra), the group that carried leaf-rust resistance into many modern varieties.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Brazil around 1915, Guatemala in the 1940s, then Central America and Colombia
body: Caturra was found in Minas Gerais, Brazil, between 1915 and 1918; its name comes from a Guaraní word for “small”. It reached Guatemala in the 1940s, though it wasn't widely planted there for about 30 years; it later spread to Costa Rica, Honduras and Panama, and was once thought to make up nearly half of Colombia's coffee.
Leaf rust changed that. By 2015 Colombia had replaced about 3.3 billion trees with rust-resistant varieties such as Castillo.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Compact, medium yield, very weak to leaf rust
body: A dwarf tree with green leaf tips, average-size beans and a medium yield. It's very susceptible to coffee leaf rust, a fungus that can cause severe crop losses.
World Coffee Research calls it standard quality in Central America and rates its cup potential up high as good; it does best above about 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator.

entries.name: Gesha
entries.summary: An Ethiopian coffee that became the star of Panama's auctions.
entries.lede: A tall, low-yielding coffee collected from Ethiopia's forests in the 1930s. It passed through research stations in Tanzania and Costa Rica and sat ignored in Panama for decades, until a farm there entered it in a competition in the mid-2000s.

facts.label: collected from Ethiopia's coffee forests
its number at CATIE, Costa Rica, from 1953

taste.text: World Coffee Research describes delicate floral, jasmine and peach-like aromas from Gesha that's well grown, high up. One roaster describes Panamanian Gesha as light and tea-like in body.
taste.label: tendency
taste.evidence: That's for the true Panama line, grown high. Many coffees sold as Gesha are something else by DNA.

myths.claim: Every “Gesha” is the famous Panama coffee.
myths.text: In a 2020 DNA study, only 39% of 88 samples sold as Gesha matched the reference Gesha. The name is also used for other, mostly Ethiopian coffees.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: An Ethiopian landrace, outside the Typica and Bourbon lines
body: World Coffee Research places Gesha among the Ethiopian landraces: coffees collected from Ethiopia, Arabica's main center of genetic diversity. The Panama line descends from one accession, T2722, and is uniform.
Gesha Village, a farm in Ethiopia, grows its own selections from the Gori Gesha forest, sold under names like “Gesha 1931”. No published DNA comparison with the Panama line exists.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Ethiopia, Tanzania, Costa Rica, Panama, then a record in the mid-2000s
body: Seeds were collected in Ethiopia's coffee forests in the 1930s (sources give different years) and grown at the Lyamungu research station in Tanzania. In 1953 they went to CATIE in Costa Rica, where they were logged as T2722.
In the 1960s CATIE spread it around Panama for its tolerance of leaf rust, but farmers didn't take to it: its branches are brittle.

In the mid-2000s the Peterson family of Hacienda La Esmeralda in Boquete entered it in the Best of Panama competition, and it set a record of over $20 a pound. Prices kept climbing: a washed Gesha from La Esmeralda sold for $30,204 a kilo at Best of Panama 2025.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Tall, low yield, needs altitude
body: A tall tree with green or bronze leaf tips and average beans. Yield is low, and the first crop comes in its fourth year. It has intermediate resistance to leaf rust and is susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny worms that attack the roots).
World Coffee Research recommends high altitude, above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, and rates its cup potential there as exceptional.

sections.title: Gesha or Geisha?
sections.teaser: Same coffee, two spellings
body: “Geisha” is how it first appeared in records. Many people now write “Gesha”, after the area in Ethiopia it's named for.

entries.name: SL28
entries.summary: Kenya's famous 1930s selection, from a drought-tolerant tree.
entries.lede: One tree picked out in 1935 by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in Kenya, from a drought-tolerant population collected in Tanganyika, today's Tanzania. With SL34 it became one of Kenya's benchmark varieties.

facts.label: picked from a single tree in Kenya
its family by DNA (SL34 tests as Typica)
old trees in Kenya still bear coffee
where it does best near the equator (3,940 ft)

taste.text: Roasters describe blackcurrant and dark berry, citrus, a wine-like acidity and a juicy finish. One calls these tendencies rather than a fixed recipe.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: Kenya's altitude and careful washing are part of that taste too. When Kenya's coffee research institute (KALRO) cupped SL28 beside 30 other varieties at two sites over the 2021 and 2022 harvests, Batian scored highest overall and SL28 stood out mainly at one site (Ruiru), so place and year move its cup; how much of the classic Kenya taste comes from the variety still isn't pinned down.

myths.claim: SL28 and SL34 are both “Kenyan Bourbons”.
myths.text: By DNA only SL28 sits in the Bourbon group. SL34 tests as Typica, which suggests the “French Mission” label on its mother tree was wrong.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Bourbon by DNA; a parent of Kenya's newer varieties
body: Genetic tests put SL28 in the Bourbon group. Its usual partner on Kenyan bags, SL34, tests as Typica, so the pair aren't one family.
SL28 is in the ancestry of the newer, disease-resistant Kenyan varieties Ruiru 11 and Batian.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Scott Labs, 1935, from Tanganyika seed
body: The British colonial government set up Scott Agricultural Laboratories in Kenya in 1922. Between 1935 and 1939 it evaluated 42 trees; SL28 came from one tree of the “Tanganyika Drought Resistant” population, which coffee officer A.D. Trench spotted on a 1931 tour of Tanganyika; seed was brought back to Scott Labs.
It later spread to Uganda, other parts of Africa and Latin America. In 2017 Dale Harris won the World Barista Championship with a washed SL28 from El Salvador.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Tall, drought-tolerant, low yield, weak to disease
body: A tall tree whose branches droop with age. Its beans are large and it gives a lot of green coffee per cherry, but its yield is low. It needs little fertilizer and copes with drought, but is susceptible to leaf rust, coffee berry disease and nematodes.
It's most common in Kenya, Malawi, Uganda and Zimbabwe.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: AA is a size; a Kenyan lot may mix varieties
body: Kenyan grades like AA and AB are bean sizes, not varieties or cup scores. A Kenyan lot sold as SL28 may also contain SL34, Ruiru 11 or Batian, and SL-derived trees have drifted genetically over the years.

entries.name: Washed
entries.summary: Fruit off, fermented, then washed clean before drying.
entries.lede: The fruit is pulped off the seed, the sticky layer left behind is fermented away in tanks, and the beans are rinsed before they dry.

stepsText.text: A machine strips off the skin and pulp. The sticky mucilage left on the parchment (the papery shell around the seed) ferments in tanks for 12 to 72 hours while microbes break its sugars down, and then it's rinsed off before the beans dry.

taste.text: Clean, bright and crisp, with pronounced acidity and a lighter body than a natural.
taste.label: tendency
taste.evidence: In a Brazilian trial of 11 varieties, washed scored the same as or higher than natural for all 11, by about 0.4 to 6.4 points.

tips.text: Some baristas grind washed coffees a little finer than naturals. That's habit, not tested science, so your own best shot wins.
tips.label: anecdotal

kinds.name: Kenyan double ferment
kinds.text: After washing, the beans soak under clean water before drying, a habit from Kenya.

kinds.name: Anaerobic washed
kinds.text: Fermented sealed in tanks first, then washed. Leaner and brighter, with a tangy edge.

kinds.name: Extended fermentation
kinds.text: A longer ferment than usual; one Colombian producer goes past 80 hours.

kinds.name: Demucilaged
kinds.text: A machine scrubs the sticky fruit off instead of a ferment; in Brazil it's often called semi-washed.

myths.text: Usually it is: unless a machine scrubs it off, the sticky fruit layer ferments off in tanks before the rinse. Nearly all coffee ferments somewhat on its way to the bag.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: Roasting it
sections.teaser: Takes heat well; underdeveloped lots taste sour
body: Washed coffees take heat well and can handle a longer roast. Underdeveloped washed batches taste sour.

entries.name: Natural
entries.summary: Dried whole, with the fruit still on.
entries.lede: The whole cherry dries with the seed still inside, like a raisin around a pit. It's used mainly in dry places such as Ethiopia and Brazil, and tends to taste deep and fruity.

stepsText.text: Cherries often dry on raised beds. The fruit ferments during the first days of drying; drying then continues until the seed is down to about 11–12% water. When the wrong microbes take over and the fruit molds or rots, the cup turns unpleasant; drying fast in machines stops most of that fermentation.

taste.text: Berry, stone-fruit or dried-fruit notes and a heavier body than the same coffee washed. It can turn wine-like or brandy-like; when the fruit rots, the cup goes bad.
taste.label: tendency
taste.evidence: Importers and reviewers agree on the style. In one trial of 11 varieties, washed scored the same or higher for all of them: naturals taste different, not automatically better.

tips.text: Baristas often grind naturals a little coarser. That's habit, not tested science, so your own best shot wins.
tips.label: anecdotal

kinds.name: Anaerobic natural
kinds.text: Sealed in a tank first. Intense fruit, often with a lactic, yogurt-like tang.

kinds.name: Carbonic maceration
kinds.text: Fermented in tanks filled with CO2, an idea borrowed from winemaking.

kinds.name: Slow dry
kinds.text: Drying stretched out, to 60 days or more in some anaerobic naturals.

kinds.name: Ethiopian natural
kinds.text: Ethiopia sells both washed and natural coffees. Bags often add a grade like Gr1 or G1.

myths.claim: The fruit's sugars soak into the bean.
myths.text: You'll read it on bags, but none of the studies we found measured it. One study of washed fermentation suggests sugars may leak out of the bean instead. The fruit notes are real; how they get there isn't settled.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: Roasting it
sections.teaser: Browns faster, so roasters often go lighter
body: Leftover sugars make naturals take on color more quickly, so roasters often roast them lighter than washed coffees. Natural green coffee is often less dense than washed, too.

entries.name: Honey
entries.summary: Skin off, some of the sticky fruit left on to dry.
entries.lede: A middle path between washed and natural: the skin and pulp come off, but some or all of the sticky mucilage stays on the seed while it dries. In Brazil the same idea is called pulped natural.

stepsText.text: How much mucilage stays, and how it dries, gives the colors. Yellow honey has part of it removed by machine and dries golden; red honey keeps all of it; black honey also keeps it all, uses very sweet fruit from the peak of harvest and dries darkest, taking the longest. Mills use the names differently, so treat the colors as a rough guide.

taste.text: Rounder acidity than washed, with less citrus and more chocolate and sweetness, says one long-running review site; a roaster calls it silky and honey-like.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: Honey lots vary a lot; one veteran reviewer suspects most of the difference comes from how they were dried.

kinds.name: Yellow honey
kinds.text: Part of the mucilage removed by machine; dries a dark yellow.

kinds.name: Red honey
kinds.text: All the mucilage left on; dries reddish.

kinds.name: Black honey
kinds.text: All of it left on, from very sweet peak-harvest fruit; dries darkest and slowest.

kinds.name: Pulped natural
kinds.text: Brazil's name for it, from about the 1990s; virtually all the pulp stays on.

myths.claim: A darker honey always tastes sweeter.
myths.text: One veteran reviewer suspects drying explains most of the difference between honey lots, and mills use the color names differently.
myths.label: unproven

entries.name: Colombia
entries.summary: Half a million growers, two harvests a year, high in the Andes.
entries.lede: Three Andean mountain ranges, two harvests a year and more than half a million growers, nearly all on small farms. Most of its coffee land is now planted with rust-resistant varieties, and its production has shifted southwest, toward Huila, Cauca and Nariño.

harvestText.text: Timing shifts by department and altitude: central areas pick heavily in April–June and September–December, and the smaller mitaca crop comes about six months after the main one. Between its departments and the two crops, Colombia picks coffee in most months of the year. A crop usually reaches roasters a few months after it's picked: it rests 30–60 days, then spends about six weeks at sea. Sources differ on Huila: Barista Hustle puts southern Huila's main crop in August–December and its second crop in March–June, while Cafe Imports gives Huila a November–January main crop and a May–July fly crop, and the reverse for Cauca and Nariño.

grows.text: Almost all washed on the farm. Naturals, honeys and experimental lots (anaerobic, thermal shock, co-ferments, lactic, koji) are a small specialty niche: about 15,000 70-kg bags a year by a 2021 estimate, against about 10.7 million exported in 2020. Rust-resistant varieties cover 88% of coffee land (2025); Castillo was used to replant more than three billion trees from 2008, but no published split ranks them. Varieties after Castillo are in no ranked order. The nearest clue is seed: of the 82,273 kg Cenicafé's stations produced and handed out in 2020, Cenicafé 1 was 41% and the Castillo lines together 48% (Castillo General 29%, Castillo El Tambo 14%, regional Castillos 5%). Typica, the only variety grown from 1938 to 1960, and Bourbon are still on Cafe Imports' list of common varieties.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Record prices in 2025; long rains trimmed the crop
body: Colombia grew 13.7 million 60-kg bags in 2025, down 2.3% after long rains early in the year, and exported 13.14 million bags worth about US$6.5 billion. The New York price for Arabica averaged 368 US cents a pound in 2025, up 56% on 2024.
USDA expects 13.4 million bags in 2026/27.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
sections.teaser: Small farms and the national growers' federation
body: 97% of Colombia's 561,766 growers farm 5 hectares or less. The national growers' federation (FNC) buys coffee across the country; its 2025 purchases split 41.6% north, 29.6% center and 28.8% south. Its research arm, Cenicafé, bred Castillo.
The United States buys nearly 40% of Colombia's exports.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: Supremo and Excelso are bean sizes, not quality
body: Supremo and Excelso are size grades: Supremo is the bigger beans, Excelso the smaller. Sources disagree on the exact screen sizes, so we leave the numbers out.
Huila coffee has carried a protected Denomination of Origin since 2013.

feel.acidity: medium to bright; softer in the north

entries.name: Ethiopia
entries.summary: Where Arabica comes from. Washed runs floral, natural berry and heavy.
entries.lede: Arabica was born in Ethiopia's forests, and the country holds more of the species' genetic variety than anywhere else. Most of its growers are smallholders, much of it grown in gardens and semi-wild forest, and it's sold both washed and natural, though most of it, about 70–80%, is natural (sun-dried).

grows.text: Mostly natural: about 70–80% sun-dried and 20–30% washed (UNIDO, 2025), with a few honey and anaerobic lots. The trees are mostly local landraces sold as “heirloom”, plus research-center selections like 74110 and 74112; Ethio Coffee calls those selections a small share, though USDA says over half the coffee area was replanted with higher-yielding varieties in four years.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Record crops and exports; stricter export rules
body: USDA expects a record 12.1 million bags in 2026/27, after more than half the coffee area was replanted with higher-yielding varieties over four years. Export earnings reached a record US$3.0 billion in the 2025/26 fiscal year.
A September 2025 rule (ECTA Directive 1106/2025) raised exporters' minimum capital and requires every exporter who isn't a farmer to run a certified lab with a qualified taster.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
sections.teaser: From a commodity exchange back toward traceable lots
body: From 2008 most coffee went through the Ethiopian Commodity Exchange (ECX), which pooled it by region and made it hard to trace to a farm. Reforms since 2017 set out to restore traceability, cut blending and let more producers export directly.
Bags often read region, washing station, grade and process, like “Yirgacheffe Aricha Gr1 Natural”.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: Grades 1 to 5; “heirloom” isn't one variety
body: Grades run from 1, the fewest defects, to 5, set by the number of defects in a sample. Sources give slightly different cutoffs: 1Zpresso puts Grade 2 at 5–12 defects, while StoneX allows up to 13 secondary defects in a 350 g sample.

“Heirloom” or “landrace” covers Ethiopia's many local coffee types, which haven't all been catalogued. Numbers like 74110 and 74112 are selections released by the Jimma research center in the late 1970s.

feel.body: lighter when washed, full and syrupy when natural

entries.name: Kenya
entries.summary: Washed SL28 and SL34, sold at a weekly auction in Nairobi.
entries.lede: Kenya's coffee is mostly washed, about 80% of it sold through cooperatives, and much of it is sold at the Nairobi Coffee Exchange's weekly auction. It's known for bright, juicy cups, which roasters tie to its SL28 and SL34 trees, its altitude and its careful washing.

harvestText.text: The main crop is picked from October to December, sometimes into January, and some areas pick a smaller “fly crop” from June to August. At a US importer, main-crop Kenyans arrive about May to August and fly-crop coffee about November to March. Other sources put the smaller crop a little earlier: May to July in central Kenya (Sucafina) or May to August (Starbucks).

grows.species: Arabica (over 90% of the coffee area by a 2014 research count; USDA counts only Arabica)
grows.text: Mostly fully washed, Kenya's long-ferment style; naturals are mainly lower grades and coffee for home use, with some specialty lots. Most farms grow a mix of SL28 and SL34 with Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian; no official shares exist.

sections.title: How it's washed
sections.teaser: Long ferments, washing channels, a soak
body: The classic Kenyan way: cherries are pulped and sorted into streams by density, fermented overnight and then up to about 36 hours with water changes, washed in channels, soaked for 12 to 48 hours and dried on raised beds. Naturals exist too.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Record auction prices, then a slide; a new Coffee Act
body: Auction prices hit a record average of KES 1,025 a kilo (about US$7.91) in September 2025, then slid: by April 2026 they averaged about US$269 per 50 kg bag, 28% below October 2025. Between October 2025 and May 2026 the auction sold 602,973 bags. USDA expects 950,000 bags in 2026/27, up about 12%.

A new system to pay farmers directly through a bank was suspended by the High Court until May 2026, on a petition by coffee farmers. In March 2026 a new Coffee Act moved oversight to a revived Coffee Board of Kenya, set up a separate coffee research institute, and wrote a digital direct-payment system for farmers into law. By June 2026 the system had been built into the Nairobi exchange's trading platform, and the reform committee's term was extended to June 2027.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
sections.teaser: The weekly auction, or direct sales outside it
body: The Nairobi Coffee Exchange has held auctions since 1935, by USDA's and Royal Coffee's dates (Ozone Coffee gives 1934). About 50 licensed exporters cup samples and bid through agents. Independent marketing agents have been allowed since the early 2000s, and since 2006 buyers can also purchase directly, outside the auction.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: AA and AB are bean sizes; PB is peaberry
body: Kenyan grades are about bean size, not cup quality: AA is the biggest of the usual grades, AB a bit smaller, and PB the peaberries, cherries that grew one round seed instead of two. Sources give slightly different screen sizes for each grade.

harvestText.text: Picked from about April to September, peaking June to August. Coffee picked mid-year reaches buyers later in the year, after resting 30–60 days and about six weeks at sea. Cafe Imports gives June–September; USDA said in 2022 that picking starts in April and that about 85% of the crop is picked between April and July.

grows.text: Mostly washed on the farm; naturals and honeys are a small specialty share, though they took 7 of the 32 Cup of Excellence places in 2025. Most trees are now Catimor, planted after the 2012–13 rust epidemic; Typica, the traditional variety, Caturra, Bourbon and Pache follow, in no ranked order, and Gesha leads in competitions. Cafe Imports also lists Mundo Novo among Peru's common varieties. USDA's 2022 annual gave a different split, over 70% Typica and 20% Caturra, which conflicts with World Coffee Research's 2025 account that most trees are now Catimor; no newer survey ranks them. No published figure gives the washed share by volume, and in 2016 the old natural coco process was still used alongside washing.

sections.teaser: A steady crop of about 4.8 million bags

sections.title: Cup of Excellence
sections.teaser: Cajamarca and Cusco keep winning
body: Peru's Cup of Excellence winners came from Cajamarca in 2017, 2019 and 2022 to 2025, and from Cusco in 2018, 2020 and 2021.

feel.acidity: bright in top lots, often low in everyday ones

entries.name: Bourbon
entries.summary: One of Arabica's two old lines, named for Bourbon Island.
entries.lede: One of the two historic lines of cultivated Arabica, alongside Typica. French missionaries took it from Yemen to Bourbon Island, today's Réunion, in the early 1700s, and it reached Brazil around 1860.

facts.label: where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)
from tall trees with average-size beans
on most Latin American farms by Caturra, Catuaí and Mundo Novo
Guatemala, Honduras and Peru still grow it

taste.text: Roasters describe caramel and milk-chocolate sweetness with a rounded body, and, when it's grown high, a lift of stone fruit, citrus or flowers. World Coffee Research credits it with excellent cup quality at the highest altitudes.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: There isn't one Bourbon taste: where it's grown and how it's processed shift the cup a lot, and two Bourbons from the same country can taste very different.

myths.claim: Pink Bourbon is a kind of Bourbon.
myths.text: The name says so, but DNA tests in 2023 led a geneticist to conclude Pink Bourbon is an Ethiopian landrace with nothing to do with Bourbon. A name on a bag doesn't always match the plant.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Close kin of Typica; parent of Caturra, Pacas and Villa Sarchi
body: Like Typica, Bourbon descends from coffee grown in Yemen, and a 2024 genome study found the two closely related. Crossed with Typica, it gave Brazil's Mundo Novo.

Its natural dwarf mutations include Caturra (Brazil, 1915–18), Pacas (El Salvador, 1949) and Villa Sarchi (Costa Rica, 1950s–60s). Tekisic is a Bourbon selection made by El Salvador's coffee institute and released in 1977.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: On Réunion until the mid-1800s, then north through Latin America
body: Bourbon stayed on the island until the middle of the 19th century. From Brazil it spread north through South and Central America, mixing along the way with Bourbon-related types from India and with Ethiopian landraces.
East Africa has many Bourbon-like varieties, but none of them exactly matches Latin America's Bourbon.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Early-ripening, weak to the major coffee diseases
body: Its green-tipped trees bear their first crop in year 4, and the fruit ripens early. It's susceptible to leaf rust, coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms), which makes it hard to grow.

entries.name: Typica
entries.summary: Arabica's other old line, spread from Java to the Americas.
entries.lede: One of the two historic lines of cultivated Arabica, alongside Bourbon. It left Yemen for India and Java, and spread through the Caribbean and Latin America in the 1700s.

facts.label: WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
and very weak to leaf rust, so many farms replaced it
where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)
the Dominican Republic and Jamaica still plant it widely

taste.text: Usually described as sweet, clean and balanced, with honey or caramel notes, a smooth medium body and, when it's grown high, a clean citrus acidity.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: One reviewer who tasted many Typicas found a wide range, from red wine and chocolate in some to orchid and clove in others.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Close kin of Bourbon; a parent of Maragogipe and Mundo Novo
body: Like Bourbon, Typica descends from coffee grown in Yemen, and a 2024 genome study found the two closely related. World Coffee Research also lists Blue Mountain, from Jamaica, and Sumatra among its names.
Maragogipe, a Typica mutation found near Maragogipe in Brazil in 1870, has very large beans. Crossed with Bourbon, Typica gave Brazil's Mundo Novo.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Yemen, India, Java, Amsterdam, then the Americas
body: Typica is believed to come from southwestern Ethiopia and was taken to Yemen in the 15th or 16th century. Seeds sent from India's Malabar coast to Java in 1696 and 1699 founded it; in 1706 a single plant went from Java to Amsterdam's botanical garden, and in 1714 one went on to France.
From there it reached Suriname (1719), Martinique (1723), northern Brazil (1727), Jamaica (1730) and Costa Rica (1779). Until the 1940s most farms in Central and South America grew it.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Tall, bronze-tipped, large beans
body: A tall tree with bronze leaf tips and large beans that bears its first crop in year 4. Besides leaf rust, it's susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms) and coffee berry disease.

entries.name: SL34
entries.summary: Kenya's other 1930s benchmark, Typica-related by DNA.
entries.lede: Picked from a single tree by Kenya's Scott Agricultural Laboratories in the late 1930s, and with SL28 one of Kenya's benchmark varieties. It's grown mostly in Kenya.

facts.label: WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
lots of green coffee per cherry, and large beans
highly susceptible to coffee berry disease, a fungus of the fruit
near the equator, ideally where rain is reliable (3,940 ft)

taste.text: Roasters tend to describe it together with SL28: bright acidity, juicy blackcurrant, citrus and sweetness. Few sources describe SL34 on its own.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: Kenyan coffees taste different from one county to the next even with the same varieties and processing, so place shapes the cup too.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Typica-related by DNA, despite a “French Mission” label
body: Its mother tree was labeled “French Mission”, a name usually taken to mean Bourbon. Recent genetic tests put SL34 in the Typica group instead, so that origin story may be wrong. Its usual partner, SL28, tests as Bourbon.
SL34 is one of the parents of Batian, Kenya's newer disease-resistant variety.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: From a mission-line tree on Loresho Estate
body: By World Coffee Research's account, Spiritan missionaries planted Bourbon seed from Réunion at Bura, in the Taita Hills, in 1893, and moved seedlings to a mission near Nairobi in 1899, handing seed to settlers. Scott Labs later picked SL34 from a tree carrying that “French Mission” label on Loresho Estate in Kabete.
Like SL28, it has deep roots that let it grow without irrigation, and the pair out-yielded the older Bourbon trees they replaced.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Tall, dark bronze tips, first crop in year 3
body: A tall tree with dark bronze leaf tips, though a few strains are green-tipped, and branches that droop as they age. It bears its first crop in year 3 and is also susceptible to leaf rust and nematodes (tiny root worms).

entries.name: Pacamara
entries.summary: El Salvador's big-bean cross of Pacas and Maragogipe.
entries.lede: A cross of Pacas, a dwarf Bourbon, and Maragogipe, a Typica with huge beans, made by El Salvador's coffee research institute in the 1950s. Its name joins the first four letters of each parent.

facts.label: beans, from its Maragogipe side
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
compact trees, planted 5,000–6,000 per hectare
very susceptible, and to Ojo de Gallo, a leaf-spot disease

taste.text: El Salvador's press describes chocolate and cocoa, red berries and apricot, a bright, balanced acidity and a creamy body.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: WCR says it frequently dominates Cup of Excellence in El Salvador, and the Salvadoran press reports Pacamara scores of 90 to 93.5 there. Those are competition results, not a side-by-side trial.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Pacas (Bourbon) × Maragogipe (Typica)
body: Pacas is a dwarf mutation of Bourbon found on the Pacas family's farm in Santa Ana, El Salvador, in 1949. Maragogipe is a Typica mutation found near Maragogipe, Brazil, in 1870, known for its very large beans.
The institute's selection of the cross was never completed, so Pacamara isn't uniform: plants vary from one generation to the next.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: First crop in year 3; grown mainly in El Salvador
body: It bears its first crop in year 3 and is also susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). It's grown mainly in El Salvador, where Pacas itself makes up about a quarter of the coffee.

entries.name: Batian
entries.summary: Kenya's disease-resistant variety from 2010, now widely planted.
entries.lede: Bred at Kenya's coffee research station in Ruiru and released in 2010. It's named after the highest peak of Mount Kenya, and one importer reports it's now the country's most-planted coffee tree.

facts.label: coffee berry disease, a fungus of the fruit
its first crop after planting
beans, and lots of green coffee per cherry
unlike Ruiru 11, the dwarf hybrid before it

taste.text: One importer says it still lacks the cup that buyers prize in SL28 and SL34.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: In a 2021–22 trial of 31 varieties at two Kenyan sites, Batian had the highest overall cupping score, though the site and the taster also changed the results.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: SL28, SL34 and K7, plus the Timor Hybrid
body: Batian is a composite: a mix of three pure-line varieties. Its ancestry includes the Kenyan classics SL28, SL34 and K7, Rume Sudan, N39 and SL4, and the Timor Hybrid, a natural Arabica × Robusta cross whose Robusta genes carry rust resistance.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Born of Kenya's 1968 berry-disease epidemic
body: A coffee berry disease epidemic in 1968 cost Kenya half its production and in the 1970s the Ruiru station began a breeding program. It produced Ruiru 11, released in 1985, Kenya's most widely distributed variety from the 1980s until the early 2020s.
Batian came from single-tree selections, five generations on, from the male parent of some Ruiru 11 lines. The Coffee Research Foundation, now part of KALRO, released it.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: High-yielding and suited to smallholders
body: World Coffee Research describes it as high-yielding and well suited to smallholders. WCR calls its leaf-rust resistance tolerance and Sucafina calls it resistance; nematodes (tiny root worms) can still harm it.

entries.name: Castillo
entries.summary: Colombia's rust-resistant variety, bred from Caturra and Timor Hybrid.
entries.lede: Colombia's answer to leaf rust, a fungus that attacks coffee leaves. Cenicafé, the country's coffee research center, bred it from Caturra and the Timor Hybrid, a natural Arabica × Robusta cross.

facts.label: released by Cenicafé
of breeding, over about 15 years
of its beans grade Supremo, Colombia's large size
short trees, planted closer for more per hectare

taste.text: That's how Michael Sheridan of Catholic Relief Services, who took part in a Colombian variety cupping trial, described a good Castillo: fruity but not citric, with dark chocolate and roasted nuts. A good Caturra, next to it, was floral, with cocoa and caramel.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: One expert's words, not a measured profile.

myths.claim: Castillo can't match Caturra in the cup.
myths.text: Many quality buyers believed it, and some still prefer Caturra: in 2014 Counter Culture's Tim Hill did, decisively, while the critic Ken Davids found the two hard to tell apart blind. A cupping trial run by Catholic Relief Services with World Coffee Research and others found no statistically significant difference in average scores. Colombia's growers' federation says many comparisons pitted high-grown Caturra against Castillo planted low, where leaf rust had forced replanting.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: A blend of many lines from Caturra × Timor Hybrid
body: Castillo is a composite: a blend of many selected lines from that cross rather than a single one. The Colombia variety came out of the same kind of cross about two decades earlier.
Cenicafé also selected regional Castillos that yield more in conditions like the places they were picked in.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Bred for rust; chosen for yield
body: Leaf rust reached Colombia in the 1980s and hit hardest on farms below 1,600 m (5,250 ft), which is where Castillo replaced many Caturra trees.
When a Catholic Relief Services survey, reported in 2014, asked growers in Nariño why they preferred Castillo, 77% named yield or disease resistance; 2% named the cup.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Rust resistance from the Timor Hybrid; bigger beans
body: Its resistance to rust comes from its Timor Hybrid genes. In a 2019 Cenicafé trial it still held, though most Castillo trees showed a little rust, and Cenicafé noted that rust is starting to attack the Timor Hybrid lines in Colombia.
Selection also made the beans bigger: early versions of the Colombia variety had about 53% Supremo beans, against about 83% for Castillo in a 2006 Cenicafé study.

entries.name: Colombia
entries.summary: The variety, not the country: Colombia's first rust-resistant coffee.
entries.lede: The variety, not the country: the first rust-resistant coffee grown in Colombia. Cenicafé, the national coffee research center, bred it from Caturra and the Timor Hybrid, a natural Arabica × Robusta cross.

facts.label: released, just before leaf rust reached Colombia
a blend of related lines, not a single one
of early versions' beans graded Supremo, the large size
and “good” quality, on one roaster's chart

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Caturra × Timor Hybrid; Castillo followed from the same work
body: It was bred by crossing Caturra with the Timor Hybrid, which carries rust resistance, then refined over several generations. Unlike a single Catimor line, it's a blend of many related lines.
Castillo, released in 2005, came out of the same breeding work and has bigger beans.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Bred ahead of the rust that came in the mid-1980s
body: Caturra reached Colombia in 1952 and was widely adopted by the late 1960s. Cenicafé bred the Colombia variety ahead of an expected leaf-rust outbreak; the fungus arrived in the mid-1980s and hit hardest on farms below 1,600 m (5,250 ft).
Sources differ on the year it came out, 1982 or 1983. One roaster credits it with saving Colombia's coffee industry from serious damage.

entries.name: Chiroso
entries.summary: A Colombian variety from Urrao, once taken for a Caturra or Bourbon.
entries.lede: A Colombian coffee, grown mostly around Urrao in Antioquia, that was long taken for a Caturra mutation or a Bourbon. Early DNA work hints at Ethiopian roots instead; nothing is settled yet.

facts.label: when it was rediscovered in Colombia
what its name means: the cherries are elongated
where Chiroso is grown in Urrao, per a 2024 study (6,400–6,900 ft)
a kilo: a Chiroso lot in Best of Panama's 2024 Varietals category

taste.text: Sweet Maria's says it can be more aromatic than Bourbon or Caturra: floral, bright and tea-like. Sucafina compares it to Gesha, with more herbal notes and a fuller body.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: What importers say; no published trial has tasted it side by side with other varieties.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Taken for Bourbon; early DNA points toward eastern Ethiopia
body: A 2024 study read the chloroplast DNA, which passes only through the mother plant, of all three Chiroso types from Urrao. Bourbon Chiroso and Caturra Chiroso share a type of their own, while plain Chiroso shares Bourbon and Caturra's; as a group they sat closest to coffees from eastern Ethiopia.

Because it shows only the mother's line, and the study was small, it can't settle where Chiroso comes from. One roaster says it has been genetically identified as an Ethiopian landrace, without naming the test.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Two types; productive, weak to leaf rust
body: Bourbon Chiroso is the original, taller type. Caturra Chiroso is shorter and more compact, with red or yellow cherries; some growers believe it grows from Bourbon Chiroso's seed.
Sucafina describes both as productive and at home high up, but susceptible to leaf rust.

entries.name: Pink Bourbon
entries.summary: Sold as a Bourbon, but DNA points to an Ethiopian landrace.
entries.lede: A pink-cherried coffee from around Huila, Colombia, found growing among Bourbon trees and named after them. DNA tests in 2017 and 2023 point to an Ethiopian landrace instead.

facts.label: an importer's buyer traced its pink cherries to a farm
farmers' seed grows true, which rules out a first-generation hybrid
the one “Orange Bourbon” tested carried its DNA
some farmers see less disease than in nearby Bourbon

taste.text: Importers rave about its cup. One roaster's Pink Bourbon from Cauca tasted of raspberry, hibiscus and nectarine.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: One lot's notes, not a rule.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Not a Bourbon: an Ethiopian landrace, by DNA
body: In 2017 an importer had two plants tested, one tall and one short. Both came out most like wild coffee from Ethiopia, with partial matches to Bourbon, Catimor and a Tanzanian coffee, but the pattern looked like the importer's results for hybrids, whose best matches were only in the low 80s percent; some other coffees have matched 95–100%.

In 2023 the geneticist Christophe Montagnon tested five samples from Colombia and Costa Rica. All held Pink Bourbon DNA: one was pure, two were mixed with Bourbon and two with Catimor. His verdict: an Ethiopian landrace, not a Bourbon mutation. The importer adds that it's distinct from other landraces like Gesha.

sections.title: How it got there
sections.teaser: Maybe a breeding parent, maybe a mix-up
body: Its farmer believed it was a spontaneous cross of Red and Yellow Bourbon, since the trees looked alike and grew together.
How an Ethiopian coffee reached that farm isn't known. It may have come in as a parent for breeding, or as Gesha seed that wasn't Gesha; both are guesses.

entries.name: Ethiopian landrace
entries.summary: Ethiopia's many local coffee types, sold together as “heirloom”.
entries.lede: “Heirloom” on a bag means Ethiopia's own coffee: local types farmers selected long ago from wild coffee and, more and more, numbered selections from the national research center, usually grown together. It's a catch-all, not one variety.

facts.label: grown side by side on most farms, not fully catalogued
improved varieties released by Ethiopian research since 1978
when early numbered selections, like 74110, came out
coffee berry disease first reported in Ethiopia

taste.text: Ethiopian coffee is described by region and process more than by type. Washed lots can be sparkling-bright and citric, with floral and sweet-spice aromas; naturals lean to dried fruit, from berry to mango to peach, with a thick body.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: In one Ethiopian trial the selection mattered, and so did where it grew. Washed samples scored best at one of the three sites; at the other two, naturals scored slightly higher.

sections.title: The family
sections.teaser: Arabica's home; the world's varieties came from a slice of it
body: Ethiopia is in Arabica's native range. A 2020 study of 736 coffees found very little genetic variety in Arabica overall, with one group of wild Ethiopian coffees standing apart from the rest.
The world's cultivated varieties, Typica and Bourbon among them, grouped with Yemen's coffee and a few from the easternmost part of Ethiopia.

sections.title: Research selections
sections.teaser: Numbered picks against coffee berry disease, from 1978
body: Coffee berry disease, a fungus that attacks the cherries, was reported in Sidama, Illubabor and Kaffa in 1971 and had reached nearly every coffee region by 1978.
Ethiopia's Jimma Agricultural Research Center (JARC) answered with numbered selections such as 74110, 74112 and 74158; all seven early ones in one trial resist the disease.

sections.title: Names on the bag
sections.teaser: Kurume, Dega, Wolisho and their stories
body: Regional landraces are often named after local trees, and their history is mostly passed down by word of mouth. Kurume was identified around Yirgacheffe and is grown across the Gedeo and Guji zones; it and Dega are also found in West Guji. Wolisho is common in Yirgacheffe, Sidama and Guji, often grown alongside them.

sections.title: Growing it
sections.teaser: Forest, garden and plantation coffee, mostly on small plots
body: Ethiopian coffee comes from wild forest trees, mostly in the southwest, from trees planted around homes, and from plantations. More than 70% of producers grow it on a hectare or less, often as “garden coffee” mixed in with food crops.

entries.name: Anaerobic
entries.summary: Fermented sealed away from air, on top of any base method.
entries.lede: The coffee ferments in sealed tanks or bags that keep air out, while valves let carbon dioxide escape. It's a step added to a washed, natural or honey coffee, not a method of its own, and there's no single recipe.

steps.text: Seal it in tanks or bags
Finish as washed, honey or natural

stepsText.text: Oxygen is pushed out or used up, and the carbon dioxide the fermenting fruit gives off keeps more air away. Sealed off, the microbes work more slowly, so the ferment runs longer than in an open tank: about one to six days, and about 96 hours at one Costa Rican farm. Some producers track sugar, pH or temperature as it goes.

taste.text: Often intense: tropical or stone fruit, winey notes, sometimes jasmine or rose, and a tangy, yogurt-like edge. In one review site's tasting, anaerobic washed coffees came out a bit leaner in body and brighter than anaerobic naturals.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: That's how importers and reviewers describe it, but variety, ripeness and drying shape the cup too, so the label alone doesn't predict the taste.

kinds.name: Anaerobic natural
kinds.text: The seeds stay inside the fruit through the sealed ferment and the drying.

kinds.name: Anaerobic washed
kinds.text: Skin and fruit come off after the sealed ferment, before drying.

kinds.name: Anaerobic honey
kinds.text: Only the skin comes off afterward; the beans dry with the sticky fruit still on.

kinds.name: Double anaerobic
kinds.text: Two sealed ferments before the coffee is washed and dried.

kinds.name: Anaerobic slow dry (ASD)
kinds.text: An anaerobic natural whose drying is stretched to 60 days or more.

kinds.name: Carbonic maceration
kinds.text: Extra carbon dioxide is pumped into the tank to push out more oxygen.

myths.claim: Anaerobic means no oxygen at all.
myths.text: Critics point out that the tanks and bags reduce oxygen rather than remove it all. A fermentation consultant helped popularize “anoxic” for the oxygen-free setting itself, and the industry hasn't settled on one word.
myths.label: unproven

sections.title: How reviewers see it
sections.teaser: High scores, and a debate about what counts as a flaw
body: In a 2021 tasting of 43 anaerobic coffees, one review site scored 19 of them 93 or higher. Its editor wrote in 2019 that, judged by the standards of ten years earlier, many such coffees might seem flawed, some of them sour like plain yogurt or sour beer.

sections.title: When it goes wrong
sections.teaser: Vinegar, solvent, and a costly lost batch
body: A ferment that goes wrong can taste sharp, vinegary, solvent-like or unpleasantly savory, and for a small farm a failed batch is a serious loss. A big temperature rise in the tank is a warning that it's fermenting with oxygen after all. Warmer tanks don't automatically mean more flavor.

entries.name: Extended fermentation
entries.summary: A longer ferment than usual: days rather than hours.
entries.lede: The coffee ferments for longer than usual: days, instead of the 12 to 72 hours of a typical washed ferment. Sealed tanks slow the microbes down, which is one reason anaerobic ferments can run for days.

stepsText.text: How long is up to the producer. Sealed ferments usually run about one to six days. One Costa Rican farm ferments about 96 hours, measuring the sugar level (Brix) and stopping the ferment when it falls to a set point.

taste.text: It doesn't add one particular flavor. It turns up whatever the ferment brings, so expect a more fermented cup than the same coffee fermented briefly.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: One review site notes that, predictably, the longer the coffee stays sealed, the stronger the anaerobic effect.

kinds.name: Anaerobic
kinds.text: Sealed away from air, which slows the ferment so it can run for days.

kinds.name: Lactic
kinds.text: Steered toward yogurt-like bacteria; one leading producer gets its best lots past 80 hours.

kinds.name: Cold fermentation
kinds.text: Kept cool to slow it down; one Colombian Gesha spent three days in refrigerated tanks.

kinds.name: Self-induced anaerobic (SIAF)
kinds.text: A research term: in a closed container, the fruit and its microbes use up the oxygen, with no gas added. Trials have run from 72 hours to 5 days.

sections.title: In competitions
sections.teaser: Kept out of one award's traditional category
body: Coffee Review's 2026 Kenneth Davids Cup keeps extended or deliberately flavor-changing ferments out of its Traditional Washed category; they can enter its Experimental one.

entries.name: Carbonic maceration
entries.summary: Cherries fermented in sealed tanks filled with CO2.
entries.lede: Coffee cherries, usually whole, ferment in sealed tanks filled with carbon dioxide, which pushes the oxygen out. The idea comes from winemaking in France's Beaujolais region, and a 2015 world barista title made it famous in coffee.

steps.text: Add CO2 to push air out

stepsText.text: Extra carbon dioxide goes into the sealed tank, so the fruit ferments with even less oxygen than in a plain anaerobic ferment; “maceration” here roughly means fermentation. In one roaster's example, whole ripe cherries sat in tanks with added CO2 while temperature and yeast activity were watched, then dried in thick layers for about 25 to 35 days.

taste.text: Big fruit, a syrupy texture, intense sweetness and wine-like acidity are the usual claims. Pushed too far, it can be overwhelming.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: These are roasters' and importers' descriptions. A 2026 controlled trial on Arabica found that four of its carbonic ferments scored only slightly above the control (85.0–85.75 against 84.5).

kinds.name: Whole-cherry CM
kinds.text: The usual way: whole cherries in the CO2 tank, then dried.

kinds.name: Washed carbonic maceration
kinds.text: A version where the cherries are depulped first. One roaster says Šestić's 2015 winning coffee was made this way, citing his own account; most descriptions of CM use whole cherries.

kinds.name: Anaerobic
kinds.text: The same sealed-tank idea without the added CO2.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: From Beaujolais wine to a 2015 world title
body: Winemakers in France's Beaujolais region made it a staple for Gamay grapes in the mid-20th century. Coffee producers began trying it in the early 2010s. Saša Šestić, who had learned fermentation from an Australian winemaker, won the 2015 World Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume from Colombia, and producers in Colombia, Costa Rica and elsewhere followed.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: Often shortened to CM
body: Bags often shorten it to CM, as in one roaster's “CM” series, named after the process.

entries.name: Lactic
entries.summary: A ferment steered toward lactic acid bacteria, the yogurt kind.
entries.lede: The ferment is steered toward lactic acid bacteria, the kind in yogurt, instead of yeasts. Producers seal the coffee, usually pulped but sometimes as whole cherries, away from air; some let the bacteria already on the fruit take over, others add a bacterial culture or a little salt.

steps.text: Add a culture or salt brine

stepsText.text: Low oxygen holds back yeasts and lets bacteria take over. Producers add a lactic starter culture or a brine of about 2–3% salt, because these bacteria tolerate salt better than most of their competitors. One producer says that, compared with a natural, up to 90% of the glucose and fructose is removed from the beans.

taste.text: A creamier, velvety body, yogurt-like notes and more sweetness, with chocolate and butter in one producer's lots.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: These are producers' descriptions, and one review site notes that in the cup the line between lactic and fruity notes is rarely clean.

kinds.name: Anaerobic
kinds.text: The sealed ferment it's built on; low oxygen is what favors the bacteria.

kinds.name: Yeast-inoculated
kinds.text: The other way to steer a ferment: a chosen yeast strain is added instead.

kinds.name: Extended fermentation
kinds.text: One leading lactic producer gets its best results past 80 hours.

sections.title: In research
sections.teaser: One bacterium gave the best cup in a robusta trial
body: In a 2023 trial on Brazilian robusta, adding the lactic bacterium Leuconostoc mesenteroides gave the best-scoring cup, with caramel, fruit and spice notes, and lactic and acetic acid rose.

sections.title: Who's known for it
sections.teaser: A Colombian farm and a 2019 world title
body: La Palma y El Tucán in Colombia is a leading producer; 2019 World Barista Champion Jooyeon Jeon used its Sidra. One coffee consultant and roaster calls lactic processing a way to set a coffee apart more than a way to improve it.

entries.name: Co-fermented
entries.summary: Fruit, spice or hops added to the ferment; also sold as infused.
entries.lede: Fruit, flowers, spices or hops go into the tank while the coffee ferments, so some of the flavor in the cup comes from what was added. The names aren't standardized: bags say co-fermented, infused or macerated, often for the same thing.

stepsText.text: The additions go in with the coffee pulp or whole fruit during fermentation. Some producers also add pressed juice from an earlier batch, called mossto, as a starter. Cinnamon is sometimes added mainly to control how fast it ferments rather than for its flavor.

taste.text: It can taste clearly of what went in: a pineapple co-ferment tastes noticeably of pineapple.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: One project's data suggests only about 3% of the added fruit ends up in the cup.

kinds.name: Co-fermented
kinds.text: Natural ingredients added during fermentation.

kinds.name: Infused
kinds.text: Flavoring added after fermentation and drying.

kinds.name: Flavored
kinds.text: Flavoring added after roasting. One award draws the lines this way, but bags mix the words.

kinds.name: Mossto
kinds.text: Juice and microbes from an earlier batch of the same coffee, added as a starter, sometimes alongside fruit or hops.

sections.title: In competitions
sections.teaser: Allowed before the green stage, barred after
body: The World Barista Championship has allowed co-fermented and infused coffees since 2024, as long as nothing is added once the coffee reaches the green stage; before that, additives of any kind, added at any point, were grounds for disqualification. Coffee Review's 2026 Kenneth Davids Cup allows co-ferments only in its Experimental category and bars infused and flavored coffees. Best of Panama disqualified four coffees in 2024 as “altered from their natural DNA expression”, though one reviewer asked how that was established.

sections.title: On the label
sections.teaser: Disclosure isn't required, but it's best practice
body: For now a co-fermented coffee is treated as 100% green coffee, and US manufacturing rules don't ask for the added ingredients to be listed; one importer calls clear disclosure best practice. Allergens are an open question, and the 2015 world barista champion has called for labels that list them.

sections.title: The debate
sections.teaser: Called adulteration by some; a co-ferment topped one 2024 list
body: Traditionalists call it adulteration and worry about allergens and fairness in competitions; advocates see it as an extension of coffee's own fermentation science. One review site, which judges these coffees on their merits, named a co-ferment rated 98 its top coffee of 2024. One coffee professional expects the trend to fade and come back, and warns that small farms may spend more than they earn back; some farmers have turned to artificial flavorings, which one trade site suggests may be cheaper, since little of the added fruit reaches the cup.

entries.name: Wet-hulled
entries.summary: Parchment stripped off while still damp; Indonesia's way.
entries.lede: The papery parchment around the bean is stripped off while the beans are still damp, and the bare beans finish drying fast. It's Indonesia's way, above all Sumatra's, and it gives a heavy, earthy cup.

stepsText.text: Farmers pulp the cherries, ferment them overnight, wash off the sticky fruit and sell the wet parchment after a few hours of drying. The mill hulls it at about 25–50% moisture (sources differ), far wetter than the 10–12% at which most coffee is hulled, and the bare beans then dry on tarps or patios.

taste.text: Heavy body, low acidity and earthy, herbal, savory notes, often with dark chocolate and nuts.
taste.label: trade
taste.evidence: Importers agree on the style. Some of these notes are seen as defects in other markets, and drying the bare beans fast risks harsh, uneven drying, which is bad for the coffee.

sections.title: Why Indonesia does it
sections.teaser: A damp climate, and getting paid sooner
body: Sumatra's damp, cloudy weather makes slow drying in parchment hard, and parchment coffee that takes more than 30 days to dry shows cup problems. Hulling early also lets farmers sell sooner, which matters to smallholders in remote areas.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: “Semi-washed” means different things
body: In Indonesia “semi-washed” means wet-hulled, but in Brazil the same words mean a coffee whose sticky fruit was partly scrubbed off by machine. Indonesian bags may also print giling basah, the local name, which means “wet hulled”.

sections.title: Roasting it
sections.teaser: Often low density; the beans can look bluish
body: One importer measured a wet-hulled Sumatra at about 0.64 kg/L, low on its density scale, and the green beans often have a bluish cast.

entries.summary: By far the biggest grower: Minas Gerais Arabica and Conilon.
entries.lede: By far the world's biggest coffee grower, with both Arabica and Robusta (called Conilon here). Its heartland is Minas Gerais, where coffee grows at about 800–1,300 m (2,600–4,300 ft).

harvest.area: Sul de Minas, Mogiana, Matas de Minas

harvestText.text: Picked from about April to September, into October in some places, depending on the region and on whether it's Arabica or Conilon. A crop usually reaches roasters a few months after it's picked: it rests 30–60 days, then spends about six weeks at sea. Sucafina gives Cerrado Mineiro May–September and Sul de Minas, Mogiana and Matas de Minas April–September. In Espírito Santo, Conab says the 2026 Conilon harvest began slowly in April and was due to end in August–September; Incaper's Conilon cultivars are picked from about May (Diamante, an early one) to July (Centenária, a late one).

grows.species: Mostly Arabica (about 70% of the 2026 crop by Conab's count; USDA's 2026/27 forecast says 66%); the rest is Robusta, called Conilon
grows.text: Mostly natural: in a 2019 survey of growers, 85% dried whole cherries and 14% made pulped naturals (Brazil's honey); only 1% fermented in tanks. Catuaí and Mundo Novo are the most grown varieties; newer rust-resistant ones such as Arara, Catucaí, Obatã and Icatu are spreading (no source ranks them), and Bourbon is a specialty favorite. The survey counted growers, not bags, so it doesn't give the share of Brazil's coffee by volume that is natural; a 2024 review says naturals are especially popular for Conilon. Conilon (Robusta) was about 29% of Conab's 2026 count; Incaper, Espírito Santo's research institute, has bred Conilon cultivars such as Vitória Incaper 8142, Diamante, Jequitibá and Centenária. No source after 2012 gives each variety's share of the coffee land.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: A record crop expected; 2025's US tariff is gone
body: Conab, Brazil's crop agency, put the 2026 crop at a record 67.6 million bags in its September survey, up 19.6% on 2025: 48.2 million Arabica (up 34.8%) and 19.4 million Conilon (down 6.6%). Minas Gerais alone grew 35.6 million. Rain at flowering helped yields in Minas Gerais, while cool, wet weather trimmed Robusta in Espírito Santo.

In 2025 Brazilian coffee faced a 50% US tariff: a 10% baseline plus 40% added in July. The baseline was dropped first, then an order on November 20 removed the remaining 40%, backdated to November 13.

sections.title: New varieties
sections.teaser: Arara and Catucaí aim for Bourbon-like cups with more yield
body: Newer Brazilian varieties such as Arara (Yellow Catuaí × Obatã, released in 2012) and Catucaí (a natural Icatu × Catuaí cross, first selected in 1988) aim to pair a Bourbon-like cup with more yield and disease resistance. In a trial on 19 farms, Arara gave about 35% more cherry than Catuaí.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: Pulped natural started here
body: “Pulped natural” is a term first coined in Brazil: the skin comes off and the coffee dries with nearly all the fruit pulp still on. “Semi-washed” on a Brazilian bag means machines scrubbed off part of the pulp first; it usually tastes lighter and more delicate.

entries.name: Mexico
entries.summary: Southern highlands, from Chiapas to Veracruz.
entries.lede: Coffee grows across southern Mexico, in Chiapas on the Guatemalan border, Oaxaca, Veracruz and Puebla, mostly at about 800–1,800 m (2,600–5,900 ft). It has been planted around Veracruz since at least 1790.

regions.name: Oaxaca

harvestText.text: Picked from November to March. New-crop beans usually reach roasters in late winter or spring, so February to June is the time to look for them.

grows.species: Mostly Arabica (about 86% in the 2026/27 forecast); Robusta in the lowlands of Chiapas, Veracruz and Oaxaca
grows.text: No published national variety count is available. Sucafina names Garnica, Typica, Caturra and Bourbon as the main traditional varieties, and since 2015 about 150,000 ha have been replanted with rust-resistant ones such as Costa Rica 95, Oro Azteca and Marsellesa. Most export coffee is washed; naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are a growing specialty share. Chapingo researchers (2018) also count Catuaí and Pacamara among the most widespread varieties; Sucafina adds Mundo Novo and names Catimor as a rust-resistant choice for replanting; and Sarchimor and Anacafé 14 lots placed at the 2026 Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Output edging up
body: USDA forecasts 4.14 million 60-kg bags for 2026/27, up from 4.08 million, as Mexico’s output rebounds.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
sections.teaser: Cooperatives since 1989, and a growing home market
body: Mexico's national coffee institute, INMECAFÉ, was disbanded in 1989, and production shifted to cooperatives. Today new cafés in Mexico City and other big cities pay top prices for small, high-grown lots, so some of the best coffee stays in the country.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: SHG is altitude; EP is sorting
body: SHG means Strictly High Grown, an altitude grade also used in Mexico's coffee trade. EP, European Preparation, is a stricter sorting standard, not a flavor grade, and it has no single definition.

entries.name: Nicaragua
entries.summary: Northern highlands, five departments, small farms.
entries.lede: Nicaragua's coffee grows mostly in its northern highlands, above all in five departments: Jinotega, Matagalpa, Nueva Segovia, Madriz and Estelí. Higher farms tend to give more complex cups; lower ones face more disease and drying problems.

harvestText.text: Picked from October to March. A crop usually reaches roasters a few months later: it rests 30–60 days, then spends about six weeks at sea.

grows.species: Mostly Arabica (about 94% in 2025/26); Robusta, legal since 2013, in the southern Caribbean lowlands, and allowed since a 2016 decree in six Pacific departments
grows.text: Caturra was about 72% of plantings in USDA's 2021 count, with Bourbon, Pacas, Catuaí, Catimor, Maragogipe and Pacamara sharing the rest. Almost all coffee is washed the classic way, fermented and rinsed; naturals and honeys are a small, growing specialty share. Coffee Review and Sweet Maria's also name Typica as long established, though USDA's count doesn't list it.

sections.title: New varieties
sections.teaser: Marsellesa and Starmaya were made here
body: The research group CIRAD and the coffee trader ECOM bred Marsellesa in Nicaragua for leaf-rust resistance (released in 2009). In 2001 their researchers found a male-sterile coffee plant on La Cumplida farm: the mother of Starmaya, an F1 hybrid (the first generation of a cross between two very different parents).
In 2017 a Centroamericano, another F1, from Nueva Segovia scored 90.5 at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence; World Coffee Research confirmed the variety with a DNA test.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: A slightly smaller crop forecast
body: USDA forecasts 2.44 million 60-kg bags for 2026/27, down from 2.56 million.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: The main export crop from 1870, for about a century
body: By 1870 coffee was Nicaragua’s main export crop, and it stayed that way for about a hundred years. In 1992 more of its land was planted with coffee than with any other crop.

harvestText.text: Picked from November to April. In 2026 the Cup of Excellence jury met June 1–5 and the auction was July 16, so the year's best lots sold within months of picking. Windows vary by region: Coffee Hunter gives November to March for Copán and December to April for Montecillos, and Starbucks' origin sheet gives October to February for the country.

grows.text: No current national count has been published. In 2017 IHCAFE said 60% of the coffee area was improved, rust-resistant plants such as Lempira, IHCAFE 90 and Parainema; importers name Catuaí, Caturra, Pacas and Typica as the other common ones, and Bourbon usually comes mixed with Caturra and Catuaí. Most coffee is washed; naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are a growing experiment.

sections.title: Cup of Excellence
sections.teaser: Geisha on top in 2026; Parainema has its own category
body: At the 2026 Cup of Excellence, the top three lots were Geishas from Intibucá, Santa Bárbara and Francisco Morazán, scoring 90.39–90.50 and selling for $75–90 a pound. The best traditional lots were washed Typicas from Lempira and Pacas from Santa Bárbara.
Parainema now has a category of its own; most of its 2026 winners came from Santa Bárbara.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Growth from new planted area
body: USDA expects Honduras to supply nearly all of the region's growth in 2026/27, helped by expanding planted area and good growing conditions.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: SHG means high grown
body: SHG means Strictly High Grown, an altitude grade especially familiar in Honduras. IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, describes it as coffee grown above about 1,300 m; another guide says 1,200 m. Coffee from Copán and Opalaca can carry the protected name Honduran Western Coffees (HWC).

entries.name: Guatemala
entries.summary: Eight named regions, five of them volcanic.
entries.lede: Guatemala was one of the first countries to sell its coffee by region, and Anacafé, its national coffee association, founded in 1960, names eight. Five are volcanic regions; Huehuetenango, the highest and driest, is one of three that aren’t.

harvestText.text: Acatenango, Atitlán, Cobán, San Marcos and Nuevo Oriente pick about December to March. Across the country, picking can run from September to April, lower and warmer areas first.

grows.species: Almost all Arabica: about 98% of planted area and 96% of the crop (2026/27 forecast)
grows.text: No published national variety count is available. Only about 30% of trees resist leaf rust, and Barista Hustle says most farmers grow the traditional Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí and Pache; the resistant share is hybrids such as Catimor, Sarchimor and Anacafé 14. World Coffee Research puts Catuaí at about 20% of production. Almost all coffee is washed or mechanically demucilaged (the fruit scrubbed off by machine); naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are a small share.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: A smaller crop after borer and rust, then a rebound
body: USDA cut its 2025/26 estimate to 3.16 million bags because coffee cherry borer (a beetle that bores into the fruit) and leaf rust lowered yields. It expects 3.26 million in 2026/27.

sections.title: How it’s grown
sections.teaser: Almost all Arabica, washed or scrubbed by machine
body: Robusta is about 2% of planted area and 4% of the crop (2026/27 forecast). Most coffee is washed, or demucilaged: the sticky fruit is scrubbed off by machine instead of fermented and washed off.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: SHB means grown high, not tested for hardness
body: SHB, Strictly Hard Bean, is an altitude grade, not a measure of how hard the bean is. The cutoffs differ: one guide puts SHB above 1,350 m (4,400 ft), and an importer’s scale saves it for 1,600–1,700 m (5,200–5,600 ft), so read it as “grown high”.

feel.acidity: bright in most regions; milder in Antigua

entries.name: Costa Rica
entries.summary: Eight traditional regions, small farm mills, and the home of honey processing.
entries.lede: Coffee has grown in Costa Rica since 1779. It comes from eight traditional regions, which ICAFE redrew in 2025, from high Tarrazú (ICAFE’s Los Santos region since 2025; Tarrazú stays a protected origin name), which made about 40% of it in Royal Coffee’s 2020 count, to low Turrialba, which starts picking as early as July.

entries.regionsNote: Shares are from Royal Coffee (2020); region tastes are tendencies. These are the eight traditional regions, still the names on most bags. In June 2025 ICAFE merged Tres Ríos into the Central Valley and Orosi into Turrialba, folded Guanacaste into the Zona Norte, split Brunca into Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus, and renamed its Tarrazú region Los Santos; Tarrazú stays a protected origin name, and Tres Ríos and Orosi may still be used in promotion.

harvestText.text: Across the country, picking runs from about July to March: low regions like Turrialba start in July or August, and high Tarrazú runs from November into March. Importers quote narrower windows (October to December, or December to April), with coffee arriving from about February to July.

grows.species: Arabica only (a 1989 decree; USDA counts the whole 2026/27 crop as Arabica); two 2021 news reports say the Robusta ban was lifted in 2018, but neither names the decree
grows.text: Caturra leads ("Caturra and more Caturra," says Coffee Review), with Catuaí the other main variety. Most coffee is washed or mechanically demucilaged at mills; the micromills behind specialty lots made honey their signature and are adding naturals and anaerobic ferments. ICAFE offered Obatá, a high-yielding rust-tolerant variety from Brazil, from 2014; no published figure gives the share of rust-resistant varieties.

sections.title: Micromills and honey
sections.teaser: Farms milling their own coffee since 2000
body: Since La Candelilla opened in 2000, more than 150 micromills have followed: small mills a farm or a group of smallholders builds to process its own coffee.
Honey processing, which leaves some of the sticky fruit on the seed while it dries, is said to have started in Costa Rica. Names like yellow, red and black honey vary from mill to mill.

sections.title: Its own varieties
sections.teaser: Villa Sarchi was found here
body: Villa Sarchi, a dwarf mutation of Bourbon, was found in Alajuela in the 1950s or 1960s and is rarely grown elsewhere. Catuaí arrived in 1985 and became economically important.

Venecia is another local selection. World Coffee Research says it came from a natural mutation in a Bourbon population and was selected by ICAFE; Cafe Imports calls it a Caturra mutation. It ripens late, suits rainy zones and is very susceptible to leaf rust.

sections.title: On the bag
sections.teaser: SHB means grown high; the line moves
body: SHB, Strictly Hard Bean, means grown high: above 1,200 m (3,900 ft) by one importer’s and one guide’s line, above 1,350 m (4,400 ft) by another importer’s. GHB, Good Hard Bean, is the step below.

entries.name: Panama
entries.summary: A small producer made famous by Gesha, grown high in Chiriquí.
entries.lede: Panama is a small producer known for one variety. Gesha reached Panama in the 1960s, though few farmers planted it then, and has set auction records here since the mid-2000s. Its three main coffee regions are all high in Chiriquí province, two of them on the slopes of the Barú volcano.

grows.species: Mostly Arabica by volume: in MIDA's 2025–26 estimate Robusta was 53,000 of 170,708 quintales, though MIDA counts 6,512 of the 12,844 ha of coffee as Robusta (2026), mainly in Coclé, Colón and Panamá Oeste; mostly drunk at home
grows.text: No national count of varieties or processes has been published. Coffeeness calls Gesha the primary variety; it dominates Boquete and the auctions (40 of 50 Best of Panama lots in 2026), while Renacimiento grows mainly Catuaí, Caturra, Typica and Bourbon. Farms use washed, natural and honey processing, and Volcán leans to naturals, honeys and experimental ferments. Gesha leads in fame and price rather than proven volume: the president of SCAP, the specialty association, said in 2024 that Geisha growers are no more than 5% of the country's coffee farmers. Coffeeness says farmers in Boquete and Volcán also grow Caturra, Catuaí, Typica and, more and more, Pacamara.

sections.title: Gesha here
sections.teaser: Fussy to grow, famous at auction
body: Gesha’s cherries must be processed right after picking, and its window of ripeness seems narrower than other varieties’. The Peterson family of Hacienda La Esmeralda in Boquete made its name at Best of Panama in the mid-2000s, at over US$20 a pound.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Best of Panama 2026 averaged about $4,056 a kilo
body: Best of Panama 2026 sold 50 lots of 15 kg for US$3.04 million, about US$4,056 a kilo on average, up from about US$2,861 in 2025. The top lot, Lamastus Family Estates’ Elida Geisha Torre, went to JD.com in China for US$18,004 a kilo, below 2025’s top of US$30,204 for a Hacienda La Esmeralda washed Gesha. Auction prices are for a few kilos and have nothing to do with what a bag costs at a roaster.
From January to July 2026 China bought 10% of Panama’s coffee exports by volume but nearly a third by value, at an average export price of US$63.16 a kilo, against US$9.46 for the United States.

sections.title: Who farms it
sections.teaser: Investors, rising land prices, and Robusta in the lowlands
body: Many farms are owned by expatriates or international investors, and rising land prices often outbid local producers; Sucafina also reports illegal clearing of national parkland for new Gesha farms. Robusta grows mainly in Coclé, Colón and Panamá Oeste, with smaller areas in Darién, Panamá Este and Veraguas and only about 56 ha in Bocas del Toro (MIDA, 2026), mostly for drinking at home.

feel.acidity: bright in Gesha; mellow in Renacimiento
feel.body: light, tea-like in Gesha; fuller in Volcán

harvestText.text: Picked from about March to June, after flowering in September and October. Sources differ by a month or so: one importer says April to July, and the national tourism board February to May. Starbucks' origin map also gives April to July.

grows.text: Mostly fully washed Bourbon types: KT Press (2026) puts fully washed at about 80% of the coffee, World Coffee Research at about 62% of exports; naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are about 5% of exports. Most of the rest is semi-washed: in 2015 fully washed and semi-washed coffee were each about half of exports (IGC). Starbucks also lists the rust-resistant RAB C15 as a primary variety, though World Coffee Research says it isn't widely planted yet, and WCR names Typica alongside Bourbon among the traditional trees.

sections.title: The potato taste
sections.teaser: A one-bean defect, not your recipe
body: Coffee from Rwanda and its neighbors can carry the potato taste defect: the ground coffee and cup smell like raw, peeled potato. It’s linked to damage from the Antestia bug, only shows up when the coffee is tasted, and isn’t a health risk. At the 2013 Cup of Excellence, 51% of Rwandan entrants withdrew because of it.

One affected bean can taint a dose, so grind small amounts (about 30 g rather than 100 g), throw out a dose that tastes of it and purge the grinder with other coffee. One bad dose doesn’t mean the rest of the bag is bad.

sections.title: Right now
sections.teaser: Record export earnings and better prices
body: Exports reached 23,860 tonnes in 2025, up 39%, and the average export price rose 19% to US$6.2 a kilo. Belgium bought the most, then the United States. The government aims for 32,000 tonnes and US$192 million by 2029.

sections.title: History
sections.teaser: Missionaries, a colonial planting rule, a washing-station boom
body: German missionaries brought coffee around 1900 (sources say the late 1890s or 1904). Mibirizi, probably Rwanda’s oldest variety, is said to have come from Guatemala in the 1910s. From 1933 the Belgian colonial rulers made farmers plant coffee on at least a quarter of their land.
Reform began in 2000, and Maraba’s washing station in Huye, opened in 2001, was the first of the new stations.

stages.kicker: Hundreds of thousands of years ago
stages.title: Wild Ethiopia
stages.text: Arabica formed in Ethiopia's forests from a natural cross of two other species, Robusta and Eugenioides. Ethiopia still holds most of its genetic variety.

stages.title: Yemen
stages.text: Farming probably started here. A narrow slice of Ethiopia's diversity became the seed stock behind the world's major varieties.

stages.title: Typica
stages.text: Seeds sent to Java founded it; one plant reached Amsterdam in 1706, and from there the Americas.

stages.title: Bourbon
stages.text: Taken from Yemen to Réunion, then Bourbon Island, and on to Brazil around 1860.

stages.title: Crosses of the two
stages.text: Typica and Bourbon, mixed by nature and by breeders: Mundo Novo was found in Brazil, and Catuaí was crossed there in 1949.

stages.title: A dash of Robusta
stages.text: A natural Arabica × Robusta cross that appeared on Timor carries resistance to leaf rust. Breeders folded it into many modern varieties, starting with the Catimors.

stages.title: F1 hybrids
stages.text: First-generation crosses of distant parents, often a wild Ethiopian or Sudanese Arabica: vigorous and high-yielding. Their seed doesn't grow true, so most are cloned; Starmaya is grown from seed.

stages.title: Ethiopians in disguise
stages.text: Sold under Bourbon and Typica names, but DNA points back to Ethiopia. A ? means the evidence is early or second-hand.

species.text: Arabica is one coffee species among many. These others are grown and sold too, mostly Robusta.

processMap.about: Learn's process map (L4): where each method sits. Left to right: how much fruit stays on while drying. Bottom to top: how hands-on the fermentation is. A diagram, not a measurement.
processMap.lede: How the fruit comes off the seed. Most labels on a bag are one base method plus a few changes on top, so “anaerobic lactic natural” is natural with two changes.
processMap.note: Wet-hulled, Indonesia's way, has no dot: its fruit comes off like washed, but the beans are hulled while still damp.
